clue.text: Northern Ireland party rejected supreme god

indicators.note: To reject a thing is to throw it back, so the letters just assembled are read from the last of them to the first.

parts.note: the province's two initials, the form used on a map or a football scoreboard
a do is a party: the works do, a birthday do

explanation.surface: An Ulster political party being voted down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Northern Ireland party' reads as one political outfit and is two separate pieces, a province and a knees-up. The Norse chief is one-eyed, raven-shouldered, and gave his name to Wednesday.
explanation.definitionFit: Odin rules the Norse gods from Asgard as the father the rest answer to, which is what 'supreme' measures.

clue.text: Reduced what you did with iron?

definitions.meaning: read straight: made smaller, brought down in number or amount
read again as an undoing: the prefix that reverses a verb, set in front of what an iron takes out of a shirt

explanation.surface: A question about what an hour at the ironing board actually achieved.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter owning the second reading: no dictionary has this word meaning ironed. De- undoes whatever follows it, as in defrost and derail.
explanation.definitionFit: To decrease is to make or grow less, which is 'reduced'; and split after the prefix, what an iron does is take the creases back out.

clue.text: Losing independence, foolishly electing to pass by

indicators.note: What you lose you no longer have, so the letter named next drops out of the word before anything else is done to it.
Doing a job foolishly is doing it without order or sense, so the letters beside it will not stay as they were given.

parts.note: I is the standing short form of independence, the letter beside a candidate who stands for no party
seven letters of the word with the i already taken out, taken as they stand before the shuffle

explanation.surface: An election going badly once independence has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing independence' reads as the political disaster of the surface and is one letter leaving the raw material. That letter has to go before the shuffle, not after, or the count comes out at eight.
explanation.definitionFit: To neglect a duty is to pass it by, leaving it undone rather than refusing it outright.

clue.text: Drinks part of eggnog in silence

indicators.note: A part of something is a piece taken out of it whole, so a run of letters is lifted from the words that follow in the order they already lie.

parts.note: the run starts on the last letter of the first word, takes the whole of the second and stops one letter into the third

explanation.surface: Somebody quietly working their way through the eggnog.
explanation.walkthrough: The short words are what hide the letters: two word-joins fall inside the run and the eye reads them as gaps. Eggnog is a drink itself, which keeps the surface honest.
explanation.definitionFit: Gin is a drink and the plural names servings of it, as in two gins on the bar.

clue.text: German spoke roughly — understood?

parts.note: G is the standard short form for German, as on a school timetable
a rasping voice is a harsh, grating one, so to rasp is to speak roughly

explanation.surface: A German speaking in a harsh voice and being followed anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' sits beside a word and shuffles nothing: it belongs to the phrase that means to rasp. The dash is the setter's only signal that the sentence comes in two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: To grasp a point is to take hold of it mentally, so the past tense is what somebody who has understood has done.

clue.text: What's primarily nethermost? Absolutely dreadful, irredeemably rotten?

definitions.text: What's primarily nethermost? Absolutely dreadful, irredeemably rotten?

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes first, so each word in the list that follows gives up its opening letter and nothing else.

parts.note: the first letter of each of the five words in turn

explanation.surface: A question about something at the very bottom and thoroughly bad with it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight the sentence describes the thing; read down its initials it spells it, which is what &lit means. The word is Arabic, naming the point of sky directly beneath your feet, opposite the zenith.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a nadir is the lowest point there is, the moment when things are as dreadful as they get.

clue.text: Tickled to see commercial describing The Observer cutting Everyman

indicators.note: To describe a circle round something is to draw round it, so what comes next is set inside the letters just named.

parts.note: an ad is a commercial, the break in the middle of the programme

indicators.note: A thing cutting into another goes in among its letters, splitting it in two.

parts.note: the setter signs himself Everyman, so when he turns up in his own clue he is the first person
the paper this puzzle appears in speaks of itself as us, and the italics mark the words as its title

explanation.surface: Delight at an advert reporting that this paper has dropped its crossword setter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' reads as the advert's bad news and is the instruction to go inside. Everyman is the setter himself and The Observer the paper he writes for, so both are pronouns here.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tickled by a remark is amused by it: the same mild pleasure, well short of laughter.

clue.text: Demands and obtains one-time performers

parts.note: a one-time champion is an ex-champion, and ex stands on its own for a former anything
the turns on a variety bill are its acts

explanation.surface: An impresario demanding, and getting, the stars of a previous season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demands' alone looks like the whole definition, and the verb carries more than that: what you exact you come away with. 'Acts' is the variety-bill sense, a turn rather than a person.
explanation.definitionFit: To exact a fee or a promise is to insist on it and get it, so a fair definition has to name both halves.

clue.text: Racing damn poor, terribly cross in F1 event

indicators.note: Something done terribly is done badly, and letters handled badly come out in the wrong order.

parts.note: fourteen letters across the three words, taken as they stand before the shuffle
a cross is written as an X, the mark you put on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: A dismal weekend's motor racing leaving a spectator furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as the temper the bad racing puts you in and hands over a single letter. The race round the streets of Monte Carlo has run since 1929 and is the tightest, slowest circuit of the season.
explanation.definitionFit: Formula One's season is a series of grands prix, and the one driven through the streets of Monaco is the best known of them.

clue.text: Offering some illustration on spec, if I choose to be vague

indicators.note: To offer some of a thing is to hand over a part of it, and the part handed over here is a run of letters lying in order.

parts.words: illustration on spec, if I choose
parts.note: eleven letters starting inside the first word and running on through every gap and the comma that follow

explanation.surface: Offering an example off the cuff while reserving the right to stay woolly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On spec' and 'if I choose' are both idioms, which is exactly why a run of letters crossing them is hard to see. 'Some' is the standing signal that the letters are lying in the clue already.
explanation.definitionFit: Something non-specific names no particular case, which is what vague describes: talk that will not be pinned down.

clue.text: Communist angry before game that's seen in the garden

definitions.note: The definition describes rather than names: it says where the thing is found instead of what it is, which is fair because the plant lives nowhere else, and the wordplay settles which garden thing is meant.

indicators.note: What comes before a thing is written in front of it, so the angry word is set down ahead of the game.

parts.note: a Red is a communist, the Cold War nickname
hot under the collar is angry, and hot words are angry ones
the card game played for stakes

explanation.surface: A communist in a temper ahead of the card game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' offers sport and means the card table. The plant takes its name from the blunt iron left in a fire until its end glows, which is the shape and the colour of its flower spike.
explanation.definitionFit: The red-hot poker is a garden perennial, Kniphofia, whose tall orange spikes stand in British borders all summer.

clue.text: Frank wants extracts of vitamins in cereals

indicators.note: An extract is a piece taken out of something as it stands, so the letters come out of the words that follow in their existing order.

parts.note: the run begins on the last letter of the first word and stops three letters short of the end of the last

explanation.surface: Frank insisting on added vitamins in his breakfast cereal.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital F makes Frank a man at the head of the sentence, and the definition is the ordinary adjective. A two-letter word swallowed whole is what breaks the run up and hides it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sincere says what they actually think, which is frank without the bluntness frank can carry.

clue.text: Satirical Picador reprinted

indicators.note: A reprint sets the same letters up again, and the clue takes the licence of setting them up in a new arrangement.

parts.note: seven letters of the publisher's name, taken as they stand before the shuffle

explanation.surface: A publisher bringing a satirical book out again.
explanation.walkthrough: Picador is a London paperback imprint, which is why 'reprinted' sits so comfortably beside it. The imprint took the name from the mounted man with the lance in a bullfight.
explanation.definitionFit: A parodic piece imitates a style closely enough to mock it, which is one of satire's oldest methods.

clue.text: Put out oddest pie

indicators.note: Letters put out are letters no longer in their places, so what follows is to be set down in some other order.

parts.note: nine letters across the two words, taken as they stand before the shuffle

explanation.surface: The strangest pie of the lot being set out on the step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' reads as one phrase — annoyed, or leaving the milk bottles — and the two words have different jobs. 'Oddest' looks like a request for odd letters and is raw material instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To deposit something is to put it down somewhere, and both verbs sit unchanged in 'she put it on the table'.

clue.text: Subset of commies runs easily

definitions.meaning: read as politics: British shorthand for the hard-left faction that followed Lenin's exiled rival rather than Moscow
read as a gait instead: a horse moving at the steady pace between a walk and a canter

explanation.surface: A faction of communists having no trouble in the race.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses share nothing but a spelling: one is a nickname taken from a man's name, the other a horse's pace. 'Runs' points at the legs here, not at an election.
explanation.definitionFit: Trots is the British nickname for Trotskyist activists, one group among communists; and a horse that trots runs at an easy jog.

clue.text: Tiniest bit drunk? Extremely so

definitions.meaning: read as size: the smallest of a set of small things
read as a state instead: British slang for slightly merry, then pushed to its superlative by the two words after the question mark

explanation.surface: Somebody a fraction tipsy, or a good deal more than that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tiniest bit' reads as one phrase and the split falls inside it, the first word going to one definition and the rest to the other. Tiddly is British for slightly drunk; a tiddler is a fish too small to keep.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiddly does double duty in British English — very small, as in a tiddler, and slightly drunk — so its superlative answers both halves.

clue.text: Displayed anxiety audibly by gum!

indicators.note: What is audible is heard rather than read, so the word beside it is to be said aloud and then written down some other way.

parts.note: gum is the sticky stuff you stick paper down with, which is paste

explanation.surface: By gum, you could hear how nervous the man was.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By gum!' is the northern English exclamation the surface wants, and the clue means the adhesive. The answer is a thing you watch somebody do rather than hear, which is the joke in 'audibly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking up and down a corridor is how a waiting person shows their nerves, which is what the definition describes.

clue.text: Gauges — that sounds like fruit?

indicators.note: The phrase asks for the noise a word makes rather than its spelling, so what follows is heard and then written down another way.

parts.note: the dark stone fruit of late summer, in the plural

explanation.surface: Somebody noticing that a measuring word sounds like something you eat.
explanation.walkthrough: A silent b is the whole difference between the two, and it comes from the Latin for lead: a plumb line is a lead weight on a string, lowered to find a depth.
explanation.definitionFit: To plumb a depth is to measure it with a weighted line, so the verb gauges — it takes the measure of a thing rather than guessing at it.

clue.text: Ushered in by bears, postman refuses to change

parts.note: 'I can't bear it' and 'I can't stand it' are the same complaint
Postman Pat has been delivering letters in a British children's series since 1981, and the two words are inseparable

explanation.surface: A postman with a bear escort digging his heels in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' looks like the animals at the door and is a verb meaning tolerate. The phrase comes from draw poker, where a player keeps the hand he was dealt and asks for no new cards.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand pat is to keep the position you already hold and turn down every offer to alter it.

clue.text: Shakespearean character's far-from-bold hair

parts.note: the opposite of bold is timid, and the hyphens hold three words together as one adjective
a lock of hair is a curl of it, the piece kept in a locket

explanation.surface: The unremarkable hair of somebody in a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock is the Venetian moneylender of The Merchant of Venice, the one who asks for a pound of flesh. The apostrophe-s is joinery rather than possession, which is what makes the surface read as a description.
explanation.definitionFit: Shylock is the moneylender in The Merchant of Venice, among the best-known figures Shakespeare wrote.

clue.text: Waking up, finding topless partying

indicators.note: Something topless has lost what was on top, and in a down entry the top of a word is the letter it starts with.

parts.note: a carousal is a noisy drinking party, the noun from carouse

explanation.surface: Waking to discover that the party downstairs has lost its clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless partying' reads as one racy picture and is an instruction plus the word it works on. In a down entry the top is the first letter, so 'topless' and 'headless' would do the same job.
explanation.definitionFit: Arousal is the noun for being stirred out of sleep: the moment of coming to, rather than the state that follows.

clue.text: Raw currency

definitions.meaning: read as flesh: a graze or a bruise that hurts the moment you touch it
read as money instead: the two words printed on a banknote for what the law obliges a creditor to accept

explanation.surface: Money in some rough, unprocessed form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raw' is the doctor's sense, skin that hurts to touch, rather than the raw material the surface offers. A banknote is legal tender because the law obliges a creditor to accept it in settlement.
explanation.definitionFit: Raw skin is tender to the touch; and money is legal tender, the currency a creditor has to take.

clue.text: Twice in France, fellow admitted, big city's no laughing matter

definitions.note: The definition is a noun phrase where the answer is an adjective: 'no laughing matter' is the idiom for a thing nobody should be laughing at, which is what the answer says of a joke.

indicators.note: 'Twice' asks for the job beside it to be done two times over, so the same short word is written down and then written down again.
Somebody admitted is let inside, so the letter named beside it goes in among the letters already assembled.

parts.note: un is French for one, set down a second time at the request of the word in front
F is the standing abbreviation for fellow, as in Fellow of the Royal Society
NY is New York, which has a fair claim to being the big one

explanation.surface: A man admitted to France twice, reporting that a certain big city is grim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admitted' reads as a confession and is the instruction to go inside. The French word is the article as much as the number — un homme is a man — so the clue is only asking you to translate.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a thing no laughing matter says what unfunny says of it: there is nothing there to laugh at.

clue.text: Relative regularly ignored indigencies

indicators.note: Ignoring letters regularly means skipping them at a fixed interval, so every other letter of the word is passed over and the rest read in order.

parts.note: the second letter of the word and every other one after it, the opening letter among those dropped

explanation.surface: A relation who made a habit of turning a blind eye to poverty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indigencies' is a strained word — indigence is poverty and the plural is barely used — which is the tell that it is there for its letters. The count starts at the second letter, not the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A niece is the daughter of your brother or sister, a relative in the plainest family sense.

clue.text: Paintings with relations in wet-weather wear

parts.note: oils are paintings done in oil paint, the word on the gallery label
your kin are your relations, the word that survives in next of kin

explanation.surface: Family portraits in which everybody is dressed for the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' offers the connections between one painting and another and means the family. The cloth is cotton treated with oil to shed water, the fisherman's coat that gave the modern waterproof its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Oilskin is the stiff waterproofed cloth a trawlerman's coat is cut from, and the coat itself: clothing made for foul weather.

clue.text: A single man's part in a revolution that's mentioned in CV

definitions.note: The definition describes rather than names: it says where the thing appears instead of what it is, and the wordplay is what settles which of a CV's many lines is meant.

parts.note: a single man is a bachelor, and the apostrophe-s of the surface comes along as a letter
a full revolution is 360 of them, so one is a part of a turn

explanation.surface: An unmarried man's role in an uprising, written up on his CV.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' offers the political kind and means a full turn of the circle, which is what makes the second half read as history. A CV, curriculum vitae, is the British name for a résumé.
explanation.definitionFit: A bachelor's degree is the first university qualification, and it is the line every graduate puts on their CV.

clue.text: Quietly, I'm scared to take a look

parts.note: p is piano in a score, the composer's mark for playing softly
the squeal a comic-strip character lets out at the sight of a mouse

explanation.surface: A frightened whisper from somebody who dare not look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quietly' is the musician's p, worth learning once because it comes back constantly. The comma is the only thing separating two pieces the surface wants read as one frightened sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To peek is to take a quick look, usually somewhere you are not meant to be looking.

clue.text: And the others? Flipping tardy!

indicators.note: To flip a thing is to turn it over, so the letters just named are read from the last of them back to the first.

parts.note: et al is the Latin tag that ends a list of names, short for et alia, 'and the others'

explanation.surface: Asking after the rest of the party and being told they have not turned up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is the mild British swear word on the surface and the turning instruction underneath. Et al. is what goes after the first author's name when a paper has too many to print.
explanation.definitionFit: Tardy is the formal word for arriving after the appointed time, which is what late says of a person or a train.
